source_text: Superest illius insignissimi spectaculi ac receptissimi recognitio. munus dictum est ab officio, quoniam officium etiam muneris nomen est. officium autem mortuis hoc spectaculo facere se, ueteres arbitrabantur, posteaquam illud humaniore atrocitate temperauerunt. nam olim, quoniam animas defunctorum humaniorno sanguine propitiari creditum erat, captiuos uel mali status seruos mercati in exequiis immolabant. postea placuit impietatem uoluptate adumbrare. itaque quos parauerant, armis quibus tunc et qualiter poterant eruditos, tantum ut occidi discerent, mox edicto die inferiarum apud tumulos erogabant. ita mortem homicidiis consolabantur. haec tmunep:i origo. sed paulatim prouecti ad tantam gratiam, ad quantam et crudelitatem, quia feriarum uoluptati satis non fiebat nisi et feris humana corpora dissiparentur. quod ergo mortuis litabatur, utique parentationi deputabatur; tquae species, proinde idololatria est, quoniam et idololatria parentationis est species: tam haec quam illa mortuis ministrat. in mortuorum autem idolis daemonia consistunt. ut et titulos considerem, licet transierit hoc genus editionis ab honoribus mortuorum ad honores uiuentium, quaesturas dico et magistratus et flaminia et sacerdotia, cum tamen nominis dignitas idololatriae crimine teneatur, necesse est quicquid dignitatis nomine administratur communicet etiam maculas eius, a qua habet causas. idem de apparatibus interpretabimur in ipsorum honorum suggestu deputandis, quod purpurae, quod fasces, quod uittae, quod coronae, quod denique contiones et edicta et pultes pridianae sine pompa diaboli, sine inuitatione daemonum non sunt. quid ego de horrendo loco perorem, quem nec periuria sustinent? pluribus enim et asperioribus nominibus amphitheatrum consecratur quam Capitolium: omnium daemonum templum est. tot illic immundi spiritus considunt, quot homines capit. ut et de artibus concludam, Martem et Dianam utriusque ludi praesides nouimus.
thought_title: The amphitheater's origin in death-offerings and its demonic consecration
orientation: Tertullian is completing his survey of the shows' idolatrous elements by examining the gladiatorial show, its origin in funeral sacrifices, and the amphitheater as a temple of all demons.
pass_a_gloss: There remains the examination of that most distinguished and most received show. The gladiatorial show is named from duty, since duty is also the name of a gift. But the ancients thought that they were performing a duty to the dead with this show, after they tempered it with a more humane cruelty. For once, since it was believed that the souls of the dead were appeased by human blood, they bought captives or slaves of bad status and sacrificed them at the funerals. Later it pleased them to veil the impiety with pleasure. And so those whom they had prepared, trained in arms with which they then could and in whatever way, only so that they might learn to be killed, soon on the appointed day of the offerings to the dead they dispatched them at the tombs. Thus they consoled death with murders. This is the origin of the gladiatorial show. But gradually they advanced to as much favor as cruelty, because not enough was being done for the pleasure of the holidays unless human bodies were also torn apart by wild beasts. What therefore was being offered to the dead was certainly assigned to the cult of the dead; and this kind is likewise idolatry, since idolatry is also a kind of the cult of the dead: both this and that serve the dead. But in the idols of the dead demons dwell. So that I may also consider the titles, although this kind of exhibition has passed from honors of the dead to honors of the living, I mean quaestorships and magistracies and priesthoods of the flamens and priesthoods, yet since the dignity of the name is held by the charge of idolatry, it is necessary that whatever is administered under the name of that dignity also shares the stains of that from which it has its causes. We shall interpret the same about the apparatuses, which are to be assigned to the display of those very honors, because the purple, because the rods, because the fillets, because the crowns, because finally the assemblies and edicts and the previous day's sacrificial cakes are not without the devil's pomp, without the invitation of demons. Why should I declaim about the horrible place, which not even perjuries endure? For the amphitheater is consecrated with more and harsher names than the Capitol: it is the temple of all demons. As many unclean spirits settle there as it holds men. So that I may also conclude about the arts, we know that Mars and Diana are the presidents of each kind of game.

choices.why: The glossary requires 'gladiatorial show' for munus, and the section is explicitly about this kind of spectacle.
Tertullian is playing on the double sense of munus as both 'gift' and 'duty'; rendering officium as 'duty' preserves the wordplay.
The term refers specifically to the rites offered to deceased ancestors; 'cult of the dead' captures the ritual sense without modernizing.
Puls is a sacrificial porridge or cake offered in Roman ritual; 'pridianae' means 'of the previous day,' referring to offerings made the day before the games.
The glossary mandates 'the devil's pomp' for this phrase, which refers to the pageantry renounced at baptism.
The glossary requires 'amphitheater' for this venue, which Tertullian calls a temple of all demons.

pass_b_english: It remains to examine that most famous and most popular show. The gladiatorial show takes its name from duty, since the Latin word for the show, munus, also means a duty or gift. The ancients believed they were performing a duty to the dead with this spectacle, after they had softened it with a semblance of humanity. For in early times, since it was believed that the souls of the dead were appeased by human blood, they bought captives or slaves of poor standing and sacrificed them at the funerals. Later it pleased them to veil their impiety with pleasure. So they trained those they had acquired in whatever arms they could and however they could, just enough to learn how to be killed, and soon on the appointed day of the offerings to the dead they dispatched them at the tombs. In this way they consoled death with murders. This is the origin of the gladiatorial show. But gradually they advanced to as much favor as cruelty, because the pleasure of the holidays was not satisfied unless human bodies were torn apart by wild beasts as well. What was offered to the dead, then, was assigned to the cult of the dead. This kind of thing is idolatry, since idolatry is also a kind of cult of the dead: both the one and the other serve the dead. And in the idols of the dead, demons dwell.

Consider also the titles. Even though this kind of exhibition has passed from honors for the dead to honors for the living—I mean the political offices under which such shows were given, the quaestorships and magistracies and priesthoods of the flamens and priestly offices—since the dignity of the name is still held by the charge of idolatry, whatever is administered under the name of that dignity must necessarily share in the stains of the source from which it has its causes. We will interpret the apparatus in the same way, as things assigned to the display of those very honors: the purple robes, the rods of office, the fillets, the crowns, and finally the assemblies and edicts and the sacrificial cakes offered on the eve of the games are not without the devil's pomp, not without the invitation of demons.

Why should I speak at length about that dreadful place, which even perjuries cannot endure? For the amphitheater is consecrated with more numerous and harsher names than the Capitol: it is a temple of all demons. As many unclean spirits settle there as the place holds people. And to conclude about the arts as well, we know that Mars and Diana preside over each of the two games.

fixed: The source 'posteaquam illud humaniore atrocitate temperauerunt' means 'after they tempered it with a more humane cruelty' — the comparative 'humaniore' modifies 'atrocitate', so the English is literally accurate, but the oxymoron is intentional in the source and the suggested fix 'softened it with a semblance of humanity' loses the paradox. However, the source does say 'temperauerunt' (tempered/softened), so the edit is acceptable as a clarification of the oxymoron.
